sections.title: Basic Concept of Inequality
sections.content: In inequalities, we represent the relationship between two or more variables using symbols like >, <, =, ≥, ≤. Example: P > Q means P is greater than Q. P ≥ Q means P is greater than or equal to Q. In Level 1, the main focus is on understanding the symbols correctly and forming direct relationships.

sections.title: Direct Single-Chain Statements
sections.content: When multiple relationships are given in a single line, such as: P ≥ Q = R > S ≤ T, connect them from left to right. Example: Q = R and R > S, then Q > S. If P ≥ Q and Q = R, then P ≥ R. Always connect relationships through the middle variable.

sections.title: Two-Part Statements (Common Variable)
sections.content: When there are two separate statements and a common variable is present, connect them. Example: M > N ≥ O; O = P < Q. Here O is common. First, from M > N ≥ O we get M > O. Then from O = P we get M > P. From P < Q, the direct relationship between M and Q cannot be determined.

sections.title: Definitely True or False Conclusions
sections.content: If a clear relationship can be derived from the statement, the conclusion will be definitely true. If the relationship is the opposite, it will be definitely false. If there is not enough information, the conclusion cannot be determined. Example: A > B ≥ C. Conclusion: A > C (True). Conclusion: C > A (False).

sections.title: Either/Or Complementary Pair
sections.content: If the statement is A ≥ B, then there are two possibilities: A > B or A = B. If the conclusions are I: A > B and II: A = B, both cannot be true together, but one must be true. Therefore, the answer will be Either I or II.

sections.title: 2–3 Step Evaluation Method
sections.content: Step 1: Connect the given statements in order. Step 2: Find the common variable. Step 3: Compare the conclusion with the statement. If a clear relationship exists, it is True. If the relationship is opposite, it is False. Otherwise, it is Not Definite.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Not understanding the difference between ≥ and >. 2. Not connecting equal (=) properly. 3. Drawing conclusions without a common variable. 4. Considering both statements true in Either/Or cases.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: The main task in inequalities is to connect relationships in sequence. Linking through a common variable is essential. A conclusion is true only when a clear and definite relationship is formed.

tricks.title: Write the Chain in a Straight Line
tricks.explanation: Write all variables in sequence so that greater and smaller relationships are clear.
tricks.example: P > Q = R > S → Write as: P > Q = R > S

tricks.title: Treat Equal as a Strong Link
tricks.explanation: When there is =, both variables behave the same.
tricks.example: Q = R and R > S → Q > S

tricks.title: Think of Two Possibilities for ≥ and ≤
tricks.explanation: ≥ means > or =. So consider both cases.
tricks.example: A ≥ B → A > B or A = B

tricks.title: Find the Common Variable
tricks.explanation: Connect statements through the variable that appears in both.
tricks.example: M > N; N > O → M > O

tricks.title: Opposite Conclusion is Definitely False
tricks.explanation: If P > Q, then Q > P is definitely wrong.
tricks.example: A < B → B < A is wrong

tricks.title: Identify Either/Or
tricks.explanation: If two possibilities of the same relationship are given, the answer will be Either/Or.
tricks.example: A ≥ B → I. A > B II. A = B → Either I or II

tricks.title: Three-Step Rule
tricks.explanation: First connect, then compare, then decide.

tricks.title: When to Choose Not Definite
tricks.explanation: Choose this when no direct relationship can be formed.
tricks.example: A > B; C > D → Relationship between A and C is not definite

tricks.title: Do Not Break the Equal Sign
tricks.explanation: When variables are equal, the direction does not change.
tricks.example: P = Q and Q ≤ R → P ≤ R

tricks.title: Remember the Direction of Greater and Smaller
tricks.explanation: The open side of the symbol faces the larger value.
